evidence.text: Jesus went on from there and came to His hometown, accompanied by His disciples.
Then Jesus said to them, “Only in his hometown, among his relatives, and in his own household is a prophet without honor.”
Then Jesus called the Twelve to Him and began to send them out two by two, giving them authority over unclean spirits.
Now King Herod heard about this, for Jesus’ name had become well known, and people were saying, “John the Baptist has risen from the dead! That is why miraculous powers are at work in him.”
Meanwhile, the apostles gathered around Jesus and brought Him news of all they had done and taught.
When Jesus stepped ashore and saw a large crowd, He had compassion on them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd. And He began to teach them many things.
By now the hour was already late. So the disciples came to Jesus and said, “This is a desolate place, and the hour is already late.
But Jesus told them, “You give them something to eat.” They asked Him, “Should we go out and spend two hundred denarii to give all of them bread to eat?”
Then Jesus directed them to have the people sit in groups on the green grass.

Taking the five loaves and the two fish and looking up to heaven, Jesus spoke a blessing and broke the loaves. Then He gave them to His disciples to set before the people. And He divided the two fish among them all.
Immediately Jesus made His disciples get into the boat and go on ahead of Him to Bethsaida, while He dismissed the crowd.
When evening came, the boat was in the middle of the sea, and Jesus was alone on land.
He could see that the disciples were straining to row, because the wind was against them. About the fourth watch of the night, Jesus went out to them, walking on the sea. He intended to pass by them,
for they all saw Him and were terrified. But Jesus spoke up at once: “Take courage! It is I. Do not be afraid.”

c: Herod Antipas, sixth son of Herod the Great, was ruler of Galilee and Perea from 4
39, during the life of Jesus. His jurisdiction included the regions where Jesus and John the Baptist concentrated their ministries.

Following the example of his father, Herod Antipas founded cities. Sepphoris, his first project, was the largest city in Galilee. It was Antipas’s capital city until he built Tiberias, named in honor of the reigning emperor, Tiberius (
14–37). The city Tiberias was on the western shore of the Sea of Galilee. Antipas completed the city in
Herod Antipas offended many Jews by divorcing his wife and marrying Herodias, the wife of his half brother, Herod Philip. Antipas’s marriage to Herodias was in violation of the law of Moses (
) because Herod’s brother Philip was still alive. When John the Baptist spoke out strongly against this illegal marriage, Antipas imprisoned him (
); Herod was afraid John’s denunciation would lead to a political revolt (Josephus,

18.5.2). Later, at a banquet, Herodias’s daughter pleased Herod with her dancing, evoking a rash promise from him to give her anything she wanted. Herodias took the opportunity to have John beheaded (
It was obvious to Antipas that Jesus’ ministry was even more remarkable than John’s (see
), but he was reluctant to use force to bring about a meeting, for fear of arousing the people against him. Jesus, for his part, was openly critical of Herod Antipas (

When Jesus was finally arrested, Pilate could find no fault in Jesus, so he sent him to Herod Antipas, who was in Jerusalem for Passover. Pilate may also have been attempting to reconcile himself to Antipas. Their relationship had been rather strained since the Galilean massacre (
), and because Pilate had brought votive shields to Jerusalem that bore the image of Tiberius and were considered blasphemous by the Jews (Philo,
299–304). When Jesus was brought before Antipas, Herod only mocked him and sent him back to Pilate (
). The main political accomplishment of the incident was that Herod and Pilate were indeed reconciled (
Herod Antipas was later defeated in war by King Aretas, whose daughter he had divorced. (Jews interpreted this defeat as an act of divine judgment.) He was then deposed by Emperor Gaius in
39 and sent into exile, in response to accusations from Herod Agrippa I of Antipas’s conspiracy against Rome.
